contentBlocks.body: await response.json() returns any, and writing const product: Product = await response.json() only silences the compiler: nothing checks the server actually sent a Product. Treat every response body as unknown and parse it into your own type at the edge of the app. After that one function, the rest of your code can trust the types.

An assertion function is a handy tool for this. Its return type is asserts condition (or asserts value is T). If the function returns normally, TypeScript narrows as if you had written an if; if the check fails, it throws. That keeps a long validation readable as a straight list of checks.

Parse, do not just validate: return a new object in your own shape (trimmed strings, cents instead of floating dollars, defaults for missing optional fields). The rest of the app then never sees the raw wire format.
A type assertion like body as Product is not a check. It tells the compiler to believe you, and it is the most common way wrong data slips past TypeScript.

knowledgeItems.prompt: What does const user = (await res.json()) as User guarantee at runtime?

choices: That every User field is present
Nothing; it only changes the compile-time type
payload.answer: Nothing; it only changes the compile-time type
payload.explanation: as is erased during compilation. Only runtime checks (a guard, a parser, a schema library) can confirm the shape.

knowledgeItems.prompt: What happens after check(typeof id === "number", "bad id") returns normally?

choices: Nothing changes; id is still unknown
id is converted to a number
id is narrowed to number for the rest of the scope
payload.answer: id is narrowed to number for the rest of the scope
payload.explanation: An asserts condition function narrows just like an if statement that throws on the false branch.
